explainers.term: What a physical map shows
paras: A physical map — also called a relief map — shows the natural features of the Earth's surface. Mountains, plateaus, plains, deserts, rivers, lakes and oceans all appear, and none of it depends on human decisions. If every border in the world were redrawn tomorrow, a physical map of India would look exactly the same.

Physical maps use a colour convention you are expected to know: green for plains and lowlands, yellow and brown for higher ground with darker browns for the highest mountains, blue for water bodies, and white for snow-covered peaks. That colouring is what lets you read height from a flat sheet of paper.

explainers.term: What a political map shows
paras: A political map shows features created by people and agreed by governments: country boundaries, state and district borders, capitals and major cities. Everything on it is a human decision, which means a political map can go out of date. India's political map changed when Telangana was formed in 2014 and again when Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh became separate Union Territories in 2019.

Political maps use a different convention: each state or country gets its own flat colour so neighbours are easy to tell apart, boundaries are drawn as distinct lines, and capitals are usually marked with a star or a circled dot.

sections.h: The three things every map must have
paras: Whatever its type, the NCERT syllabus says a map has three components. Questions on this come up almost every year.
bullets: Distance (scale) — the ratio between a distance on the map and the real distance on the ground. A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map equals 50,000 cm, or half a kilometre, in reality.
Direction — shown by a north line or a compass rose. The four cardinal directions are north, south, east and west; north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west are the intermediate directions.
Symbols — standard signs and colours that let a small sheet carry a lot of information. Because symbols are internationally agreed, a map is readable even by someone who cannot read its language.

sections.h: The third type: thematic maps
paras: Students often assume there are only two kinds of map, and lose marks for it. A thematic map shows one specific theme or piece of information — rainfall distribution, population density, road and rail networks, crop patterns, or forest cover.

Thematic maps are the ones you meet most often outside the classroom: a weather map on the news, a metro route map, an election results map. They may be drawn on top of either a physical or a political base.

sections.h: Map versus plan, and what scale changes
paras: A closely related distinction is between a map and a plan. A plan is a drawing of a very small area — a house, a school building, a plot of land — drawn to a large scale so that fine detail is visible. A map covers a much larger area at a smaller scale.

Scale is what makes this work. A large-scale map covers a small area with a lot of detail; a small-scale map covers a large area with little detail. A map of your town is large scale; a map of the whole world is small scale. The wording feels backwards to most students, which is exactly why it is examined.

examples.t: Finding the Western Ghats
examples.d: Use a physical map. Mountain ranges are natural features, shown in brown shading.

examples.t: Finding the capital of Rajasthan
examples.d: Use a political map. Capitals are human-designated and marked with a star.

examples.t: Finding where the monsoon brings most rain
examples.d: Use a thematic map — specifically a rainfall distribution map.

examples.t: Finding the route of the Godavari
examples.d: Use a physical map. Rivers are natural features, drawn in blue.

mistakes: Saying a physical map shows 'no cities at all'. Many physical maps do mark major cities for reference; the point is that its main purpose is natural features.
Forgetting thematic maps exist as a third category.
Mixing up large scale and small scale. Large scale = small area, more detail.
Writing that a political map never changes. It changes whenever boundaries are redrawn.
Confusing a plan with a map — a plan covers a very small area at a large scale.

quiz.q: Which map would you use to locate the Deccan Plateau?
quiz.why: A plateau is a natural landform, so it appears on a physical (relief) map.

quiz.q: On a physical map, brown usually represents:
quiz.why: The standard convention is green for plains, brown and yellow for higher ground, blue for water and white for snow.

quiz.q: A map showing the distribution of rainfall across India is a:
quiz.why: A map devoted to one specific theme, such as rainfall, is a thematic map.

quiz.q: A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map equals:
quiz.why: 1 cm represents 50,000 cm on the ground. 50,000 cm = 500 m = half a kilometre.

applications.h: Which map a disaster response team reaches for
applications.d: When a flood hits, relief teams need both kinds at once. The physical map tells them where the river channels, low-lying plains and higher ground are, so they know which areas will flood first and where to move people. The political map tells them which districts and blocks are affected, so they know which administrative authority is responsible and where relief funds must be routed. A thematic map of population density then tells them where the most people are. This is why the National Disaster Management Authority works from layered maps rather than any single one.

applications.h: Why India's map is politically sensitive
applications.d: Because political boundaries are human agreements rather than natural facts, different countries sometimes draw them differently. India requires that maps published in the country show its officially recognised external boundaries, and the Survey of India is the authority for them. This is a direct illustration of the chapter's core idea: physical features such as the Himalayas or the Ganga are not disputed by anyone, because nature drew them. Boundaries are drawn by people, so people can disagree about them.

applications.h: Maps on your phone
applications.d: A navigation app is really several map types layered together. The satellite view is close to a physical map, showing real terrain. The default view is a political and thematic hybrid, showing state borders, city names, roads and railways. Traffic overlay is a thematic map of one variable. When you zoom in far enough to see individual buildings, the app is effectively showing you a plan. Understanding the difference between these layers is exactly the skill the NCERT chapter is teaching, applied to a tool students already use every day.

applications.h: How contour lines show height on a flat sheet
applications.d: Physical maps often use contour lines — lines joining all points of equal elevation. Where contours are packed close together, the slope is steep; where they are far apart, the land is gentle. Concentric closed contours indicate a hill, and the same pattern with decreasing values indicates a depression. This is how a two-dimensional sheet of paper conveys three-dimensional relief, and it is the technique behind the layer colouring — green, yellow, brown, white — that students are asked to interpret.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between a physical map and a political map.
boardQuestions.a: A physical map, also called a relief map, shows the natural features of the Earth's surface such as mountains, plateaus, plains, deserts, rivers, lakes and oceans. It uses a standard colour scheme — green for plains, yellow and brown for highlands, blue for water and white for snow-covered peaks. A political map shows features created and agreed by people: the boundaries of countries, states and districts, along with capitals and major cities, usually with each unit in a different flat colour. The essential difference is that physical features are natural and change only over geological time, whereas political features are human decisions and can change whenever boundaries are redrawn — as India's did when Telangana was created in 2014.

boardQuestions.q: What are the three components of a map? Explain each briefly.
boardQuestions.a: The three components are distance, direction and symbols. Distance is expressed through the scale, which is the ratio between a distance measured on the map and the corresponding distance on the ground; a scale of 1:50,000 means one centimetre on the map represents 50,000 centimetres, or half a kilometre, in reality. Direction is shown by a north line or compass rose; the four cardinal directions are north, south, east and west, with north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west as the intermediate directions. Symbols are the standard, internationally agreed signs and colours used for features such as roads, railways, bridges and buildings, which allow a great deal of information to be packed onto a small sheet and make a map readable regardless of the reader's language.

boardQuestions.q: Differentiate between a map and a plan with examples.
boardQuestions.a: A map is a drawing of a large area, such as a district, a country or the whole world, drawn to a relatively small scale. Because so much ground must fit onto one sheet, features are generalised and shown by symbols. A plan is a drawing of a very small area, such as a room, a house or a plot of land, drawn to a large scale, so it can show precise detail such as the thickness of a wall or the exact dimensions of a room. To find the route from Delhi to Jaipur you need a map; to find the width of your classroom you need a plan. An architect works with plans, a traveller with maps.

boardQuestions.q: What is a thematic map? Give two examples and explain their use.
boardQuestions.a: A thematic map is one that focuses on a single specific theme or piece of information rather than showing general features. Two examples are a rainfall distribution map, which shows how much rain different parts of the country receive and is used to plan cropping patterns and irrigation, and a population density map, which shows how thickly people are settled in different areas and is used for planning schools, hospitals and transport. Other examples include road maps, crop maps and forest cover maps. Thematic maps may be drawn over either a physical or a political base, and they are the type most often seen outside the classroom — a weather map on television or a metro route map are both thematic.

boardQuestions.q: Explain the difference between a large-scale and a small-scale map.
boardQuestions.a: A large-scale map shows a small area with a great deal of detail, because the representative fraction is larger — a scale such as 1:1,000 means very little ground fits on the sheet, leaving room for fine detail. A small-scale map shows a large area with little detail, because the representative fraction is smaller, as in 1:1,000,000 where a great deal of ground must be compressed onto one sheet. A plan of a building uses a large scale; a map of the world uses a very small scale. The terms often feel reversed to students, so it helps to remember that they describe the size of the fraction, not the size of the area covered.

assertionReason.assertion: Political maps need to be revised more often than physical maps.
assertionReason.reason: Political boundaries are decided by governments and can change.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Boundaries change with administrative decisions, as when Telangana was formed in 2014, while mountains and rivers change only over geological timescales.

assertionReason.assertion: A plan can show the width of a single wall but a map cannot.
assertionReason.reason: A plan is drawn to a large scale covering a very small area.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. The large scale of a plan leaves enough room on the sheet to represent very small features accurately, which a small-scale map cannot do.

assertionReason.assertion: A sketch is a type of map.
assertionReason.reason: A sketch is drawn to scale using standard symbols.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is broadly acceptable as a rough drawing of an area, but the reason is false — a sketch is specifically NOT drawn to scale, which is exactly what distinguishes it from a map or a plan.

assertionReason.assertion: Blue is used on physical maps to show water bodies.
assertionReason.reason: Physical maps follow a standard colour convention to indicate relief and water.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The convention is green for plains, yellow and brown for highlands, white for snow and blue for water.

glossary.def: A representation of the Earth's surface, or part of it, drawn on a flat sheet according to a scale.
A map showing natural features such as mountains, plateaus, plains, rivers and oceans. Also called a relief map.
A map showing human-made divisions — countries, states, districts, boundaries, capitals and cities.
A map devoted to one specific theme, such as rainfall, population density, roads or crops.
A drawing of a very small area on a large scale, showing fine detail such as room dimensions.
A rough drawing of an area based on memory and observation, NOT drawn to scale.
The ratio between a distance measured on the map and the corresponding actual distance on the ground.
A map covering a small area with a lot of detail, using a large representative fraction such as 1:1,000.
A map covering a large area with little detail, using a small representative fraction such as 1:1,000,000.
A line on a map joining all points of equal elevation. Closely spaced contours indicate a steep slope.
The four main directions — north, south, east and west — shown on a map by a compass rose or north line.
A true three-dimensional model of the Earth, accurate in shape and size but unable to show small areas in detail.

revision: Physical map = NATURAL features (mountains, rivers, plains). Political map = HUMAN-MADE divisions (countries, states, capitals).
Third type: THEMATIC map — one theme only, such as rainfall, population or roads. Do not forget it.
Three components of every map: DISTANCE (scale), DIRECTION (north line), SYMBOLS.
Physical map colours: green = plains, yellow/brown = highlands, blue = water, white = snow.
Plan = very small area, LARGE scale, high detail. Map = large area, smaller scale, generalised.
Sketch = NOT to scale. That is the single fact that separates it from a plan and a map.
Large scale = SMALL area, MORE detail. Small scale = LARGE area, LESS detail. It feels backwards; it is not.
Political maps change (Telangana 2014, J&K and Ladakh 2019). Physical maps effectively do not.

extraFaqs.q: What are the three types of maps?
extraFaqs.a: Physical maps show natural features such as mountains, plateaus, plains and rivers. Political maps show human-made divisions such as countries, states, boundaries and capitals. Thematic maps show one particular theme, such as rainfall, population density or road networks.

extraFaqs.q: Why do political maps change but physical maps rarely do?
extraFaqs.a: Political maps record boundaries agreed by governments, and those decisions change — India's map changed when Telangana was created in 2014. Physical maps record natural features such as mountains and rivers, which change only over geological timescales.

extraFaqs.q: What are the three components of a map?
extraFaqs.a: Distance (shown by the scale), direction (shown by a north line or compass rose) and symbols (standard signs and colours). All three must be present for a map to be read correctly.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a map and a globe?
extraFaqs.a: A globe is a true three-dimensional model of the Earth, so shapes and sizes stay accurate, but it cannot show small areas in detail and is awkward to carry. A map is flat, so some distortion is unavoidable, but it can show a small area in great detail and is easy to fold, print and compare.

evaporation-and-sublimation.ncertRef: NCERT Class 9 Science, Chapter 1 — Matter in Our Surroundings.

explainers.term: Evaporation: liquid to gas, from the surface only
paras: Evaporation is a liquid changing into vapour at temperatures below its boiling point. The key idea is that it happens only at the surface. Particles in a liquid move at a range of speeds; a few at the surface happen to be moving fast enough to escape the attraction of their neighbours and leave as vapour. This is why a puddle dries at 30 °C even though water boils at 100 °C.

Because the fastest particles are the ones that escape, the average energy of the particles left behind falls — and lower average energy means lower temperature. That is why evaporation causes cooling. It is why you feel cold stepping out of a swimming pool, why sweating cools you down, and why water stays cool in an earthen pot: water seeps through the pores, evaporates from the outside, and takes heat from the pot with it.

explainers.term: Sublimation: solid straight to gas
paras: Sublimation is a solid changing directly into vapour without ever becoming a liquid. The liquid state is skipped entirely, and that single fact is the whole difference. Camphor left in a cupboard shrinks and disappears without ever leaving a puddle; naphthalene balls behave the same way.

The standard laboratory demonstration uses ammonium chloride heated in an inverted funnel over a china dish: the solid turns straight to vapour, rises, and re-forms as a solid on the cool glass above. Iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) also sublime — dry ice is named for exactly this reason, since it leaves no liquid behind.

sections.h: The four factors that speed up evaporation
paras: This list is examined directly almost every year. Learn all four with a reason for each.
bullets: Surface area — more exposed surface means more particles positioned to escape. Clothes spread out dry faster than clothes bundled up.
Temperature — heat gives particles more kinetic energy, so more of them can break free. Clothes dry faster in the sun.
Humidity — humidity is how much water vapour the air already holds. When the air is nearly saturated, evaporation slows. This is why clothes take so long to dry during the monsoon.
Wind speed — moving air carries away the vapour that has just formed, keeping the air above the liquid unsaturated so more can evaporate. Clothes dry faster on a breezy day.

sections.h: All six changes of state, and their names
paras: Naming the reverse processes correctly separates a full-mark answer from a partial one.
bullets: Melting (fusion) — solid to liquid, at the melting point.
Freezing (solidification) — liquid to solid, the reverse of melting.
Vaporisation — liquid to gas. This covers both evaporation (at the surface, any temperature) and boiling (throughout the liquid, at the boiling point only).
Condensation — gas to liquid, the reverse of vaporisation. Dew on grass, water droplets on a cold glass.
Sublimation — solid straight to gas.
Deposition (also called desublimation) — gas straight to solid, the reverse of sublimation. Frost forming on a cold window is water vapour depositing as ice.

sections.h: Why latent heat matters here
paras: During a change of state, heat is absorbed or released but the temperature does not change. That hidden heat is called latent heat, and it goes into overcoming the forces holding the particles together rather than into raising temperature.

The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg and the latent heat of vaporisation of water is 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg. The vaporisation figure is far larger because the particles must be separated completely, not merely loosened. This is why steam at 100 °C causes a much worse burn than water at 100 °C: the steam releases all that extra latent heat as it condenses on your skin.

examples.t: Wet clothes drying on a line
examples.d: Evaporation. Liquid water at the fabric's surface becomes vapour well below 100 °C.

examples.t: A camphor tablet vanishing over a week
examples.d: Sublimation. The solid became vapour directly — the shelf underneath stayed dry.

examples.t: Feeling cold after a swim
examples.d: Evaporation causes cooling. The fastest water particles leave your skin, taking energy with them.

examples.t: Dry ice producing white fog
examples.d: Sublimation. Solid carbon dioxide becomes gas directly; the visible fog is water vapour from the air condensing in the cold.

examples.t: Frost on a windowpane
examples.d: Deposition — the reverse of sublimation. Water vapour becomes solid ice without becoming liquid first.

mistakes: Saying sublimation is 'fast evaporation'. They start from different states entirely — sublimation starts from a solid, evaporation from a liquid.
Claiming evaporation only happens at the boiling point. It happens at all temperatures, because it only needs surface particles with enough energy.
Confusing evaporation with boiling. Evaporation is a surface phenomenon at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
Forgetting that evaporation causes cooling, and forgetting to explain why (the higher-energy particles leave).
Naming the reverse of sublimation as 'condensation'. Gas to solid is deposition; condensation is gas to liquid.

quiz.q: Camphor left in the open disappears without leaving any liquid. This is:
quiz.why: The solid turned straight into vapour with no liquid stage — the definition of sublimation.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT increase the rate of evaporation?
quiz.why: Higher humidity means the air already holds a lot of water vapour, which slows evaporation down.

quiz.q: Water in an earthen pot stays cool because:
options: Water evaporates through the pores and takes heat with it
quiz.why: Water seeps through the porous clay and evaporates from the surface; the escaping high-energy particles carry heat away, cooling what remains.

quiz.q: The change of a gas directly into a solid is called:
quiz.why: Gas to solid is deposition (desublimation). Sublimation is the opposite direction, solid to gas.

extraFaqs.q: Why does evaporation cause cooling?
extraFaqs.a: Only the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape as vapour. When they leave, the average energy of the particles remaining is lower — and lower average kinetic energy means a lower temperature. The energy needed to escape is drawn from the liquid and its surroundings.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
extraFaqs.a: Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid and at any temperature below boiling point. Boiling happens throughout the whole liquid, forming bubbles, and only at one fixed temperature — the boiling point (100 °C for water at normal pressure).

extraFaqs.q: Give three substances that sublime.
extraFaqs.a: Camphor, naphthalene (mothballs), ammonium chloride, iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) all sublime. Ammonium chloride is the one usually used in the school laboratory demonstration.

extraFaqs.q: Why does steam at 100 °C burn more badly than water at 100 °C?
extraFaqs.a: Steam carries an extra 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg of latent heat of vaporisation. When it touches skin it condenses and releases all of that energy on top of the heat from its temperature, so the burn is far more severe.

applications.h: Why an earthen pot keeps water cool
applications.d: The classic Indian example, and it is pure evaporation. Clay is porous, so water seeps slowly to the outer surface and evaporates there. Because only the fastest-moving particles escape, the average kinetic energy of the water left behind drops, and the temperature with it. The pot works best in dry, breezy weather and barely works during the monsoon, when high humidity slows evaporation. The same physics explains why desert coolers work well in Delhi in May but fail in coastal Chennai.

applications.h: Sweating, and why a fan helps
applications.d: Your body cools itself by evaporating sweat. The energy needed to turn liquid sweat into vapour is drawn from your skin, which is why you feel cold as it dries. A fan does not lower the air temperature at all — it increases the wind speed over your skin, carrying away saturated air and letting more sweat evaporate. On a very humid day a fan feels far less effective, because the air already holds close to as much water vapour as it can.

applications.h: Sublimation in the kitchen and the laboratory
applications.d: Naphthalene balls placed in a cupboard shrink and vanish over weeks without ever leaving a puddle, because they sublime directly to vapour. Dry ice — solid carbon dioxide — is used to keep ice cream and vaccines cold precisely because it sublimes: it leaves no liquid mess behind. In the school laboratory, ammonium chloride heated under an inverted funnel sublimes and re-forms as a white solid on the cool glass above, which is the standard demonstration of the process.

applications.h: Separating a subliming solid from a mixture
applications.d: Sublimation is a separation technique, not just a change of state. Given a mixture of common salt and ammonium chloride, gentle heating sublimes the ammonium chloride away as vapour, leaving pure salt behind; the vapour then deposits as a solid on a cool surface and can be collected. The same method separates camphor or iodine from sand. This is a favourite practical question because it tests whether you know which substances actually sublime.

numericals.q: How much heat is required to convert 200 g of ice at 0 °C completely into water at 0 °C? (Latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg)
steps: Convert the mass to kilograms: 200 g = 0.2 kg.
Use Q = mL, where L is the latent heat of fusion.
numericals.answer: 6.68 × 10⁴ J (66,800 J). Note the temperature does not change during the melting — all the heat goes into breaking the bonds holding the solid together.

numericals.q: Calculate the heat needed to convert 50 g of water at 100 °C into steam at 100 °C. (Latent heat of vaporisation of water = 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg)
numericals.answer: 1.125 × 10⁵ J (112,500 J). This large hidden energy is exactly why steam at 100 °C scalds far worse than water at 100 °C — it releases all of it on condensing.

numericals.q: Convert 30 °C into kelvin, and 300 K into degrees Celsius.
steps: To go from Celsius to kelvin, add 273: K = °C + 273.
To go from kelvin to Celsius, subtract 273: °C = K − 273.

boardQuestions.q: Define evaporation. List four factors that affect the rate of evaporation.
boardQuestions.a: Evaporation is the process by which a liquid changes into vapour at temperatures below its boiling point, occurring only at the surface of the liquid. Four factors affect its rate. Surface area: a larger exposed surface means more particles are positioned to escape, so clothes spread out dry faster than clothes bundled up. Temperature: heating gives particles more kinetic energy, so a greater fraction can overcome the attraction of their neighbours. Humidity: humidity is the amount of water vapour already present in the air, and when the air is close to saturated the rate falls sharply, which is why washing takes so long to dry during the monsoon. Wind speed: moving air carries away the vapour that has just formed, keeping the air above the liquid unsaturated so evaporation can continue.

boardQuestions.q: Why does evaporation cause cooling? Explain with an everyday example.
boardQuestions.a: In any liquid the particles move at a range of speeds. Only the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction and escape as vapour. When they leave, the average kinetic energy of the particles remaining is lower, and since temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, the liquid cools. The energy required for the escape is also drawn from the surroundings. An everyday example is stepping out of a swimming pool: water evaporating from your skin takes heat from your body, so you feel cold even on a warm day.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between evaporation and boiling.
boardQuestions.a: Evaporation occurs only at the surface of the liquid, whereas boiling occurs throughout the entire bulk of the liquid, with bubbles forming inside it. Evaporation happens at all temperatures below the boiling point, whereas boiling happens only at one fixed temperature, the boiling point, which is 100 °C for water at normal atmospheric pressure. Evaporation is a slow, gradual and quiet process; boiling is rapid and vigorous. Evaporation causes cooling of the remaining liquid, whereas during boiling the temperature stays constant while heat continues to be supplied.

boardQuestions.q: What is sublimation? Name three substances that sublime and describe how sublimation can be used to separate a mixture.
boardQuestions.a: Sublimation is the change of a solid directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state. Three substances that sublime are camphor, naphthalene and ammonium chloride; iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) also do. To separate a mixture of common salt and ammonium chloride, the mixture is placed in a china dish and covered with an inverted funnel whose stem is plugged with cotton. On gentle heating, the ammonium chloride sublimes and rises as vapour, then cools on the inner surface of the funnel and deposits there as a white solid, which can be scraped off. The common salt, which does not sublime, remains in the dish. The technique works whenever one component of a mixture sublimes and the other does not.

boardQuestions.q: Why does steam at 100 °C cause a more severe burn than water at 100 °C?
boardQuestions.a: Both are at the same temperature, but steam carries an additional 22.5 × 10⁵ J per kilogram of latent heat of vaporisation — the hidden energy absorbed when the water became vapour. When steam touches skin it first condenses into water, releasing all of that latent heat onto the skin, and only then does it cool from 100 °C. Water at 100 °C delivers only the second part. The extra latent heat is what makes the steam burn far worse.

assertionReason.assertion: Evaporation causes cooling.
assertionReason.reason: The particles with the highest kinetic energy escape from the surface of the liquid.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. When the highest-energy particles leave, the average kinetic energy of those remaining falls, and lower average kinetic energy means a lower temperature.

assertionReason.assertion: Water in an earthen pot becomes cooler in summer.
assertionReason.reason: Clay is a good conductor of heat.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false. The cooling has nothing to do with conduction — clay is porous, so water seeps through and evaporates from the outer surface, carrying heat away with it.

assertionReason.assertion: Sublimation involves the liquid state.
assertionReason.reason: A solid must melt before it can turn into vapour.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false — sublimation goes directly from solid to gas and skips the liquid state entirely. The reason is also a false statement about sublimation, though it is the mistake students most often make.

assertionReason.assertion: The temperature of a substance does not change during a change of state.
assertionReason.reason: The heat supplied is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. This hidden energy is called latent heat; it does work against interparticle forces rather than raising the temperature.

glossary.def: The change of a liquid into vapour at the surface only, at any temperature below the boiling point.
The change of a solid directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state.
The reverse of sublimation — a gas changing directly into a solid, as when frost forms on a cold window.
Vaporisation throughout the whole bulk of a liquid, occurring only at the fixed boiling point.
The change of a gas into a liquid, the reverse of vaporisation.
The change of a solid into a liquid at the melting point.
The heat absorbed or released during a change of state without any change in temperature.
The heat needed to change 1 kg of a solid into liquid at its melting point. For ice it is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg.
The heat needed to change 1 kg of a liquid into vapour at its boiling point. For water it is 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg.
The amount of water vapour already present in the air. High humidity slows evaporation.
Describes a liquid that evaporates readily at ordinary temperatures, such as petrol or spirit.
The SI temperature scale. K = °C + 273; 0 K is absolute zero.

revision: Evaporation: LIQUID → gas, SURFACE only, at ANY temperature below boiling.
Sublimation: SOLID → gas directly. The liquid state is skipped entirely — that is the whole difference.
Four factors speeding evaporation: surface area ↑, temperature ↑, wind speed ↑, humidity ↓.
Evaporation causes COOLING because the fastest particles are the ones that escape.
Boiling ≠ evaporation. Boiling is throughout the liquid at ONE fixed temperature.
Reverse of sublimation is DEPOSITION (gas → solid), not condensation (gas → liquid).
Substances that sublime: camphor, naphthalene, ammonium chloride, iodine, dry ice.
Temperature stays CONSTANT during any change of state — the energy goes to latent heat.

equator-and-prime-meridian.ncertRef: NCERT Class 6 Geography, Chapter 2 — Globe: Latitudes and Longitudes.

explainers.term: The Equator — the 0° line of latitude
paras: The Equator is an imaginary circle drawn around the Earth exactly midway between the North and South Poles. It is labelled 0° latitude, and it divides the globe into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

It is the longest of all the parallels of latitude, roughly 40,075 km around, because it sits at the widest part of the Earth. Every other parallel is shorter, shrinking to a single point at each pole. The Equator is a real physical reference: the Sun is overhead there twice a year, at the equinoxes, and countries on it have almost equal day and night all year round.

explainers.term: The Prime Meridian — the 0° line of longitude
paras: The Prime Meridian is the semicircle of longitude that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole through Greenwich, near London. It is labelled 0° longitude and divides the globe into the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere.

Unlike the Equator, its position is a human choice, not a natural one. There is nothing physically special about Greenwich; an international conference in 1884 simply agreed to put zero there, and the world's clocks have been set from it ever since. Any meridian could have been chosen — and before 1884, different countries used different ones.

sections.h: Parallels of latitude — the important ones
paras: There are 181 parallels in total: 90 north, 90 south, and the Equator itself. Five carry names, and CBSE expects all five with their values.
bullets: Equator — 0°, the reference line.
Tropic of Cancer — 23½° N. Passes through eight Indian states, which is a favourite exam question.
Tropic of Capricorn — 23½° S.
Arctic Circle — 66½° N.
Antarctic Circle — 66½° S.

These lines mark the heat zones: the Torrid Zone between the two Tropics (the Sun is overhead here at some point in the year), the two Temperate Zones between each Tropic and its Circle, and the two Frigid Zones beyond the Circles.

sections.h: Meridians of longitude and the link to time
paras: There are 360 meridians — 180 east and 180 west of the Prime Meridian. Unlike parallels, all meridians are the same length and all of them meet at the two poles, which is why they are semicircles rather than circles.
Longitude and time are directly connected. The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so it turns 15° in one hour and 1° in four minutes. Moving east, local time runs ahead; moving west, it falls behind.

India's Standard Meridian is 82°30′ E, passing through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Because 82.5 × 4 minutes = 330 minutes, Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time. The 180° meridian is the International Date Line, where the date changes by one day.

sections.h: The clean way to keep them straight
paras: Latitude lines run east-west but measure how far north or south you are. Longitude lines run north-south but measure how far east or west you are. Students reverse this constantly.

A memory hook that works: latitude sounds like 'ladder' — the rungs are horizontal and you climb them north or south. Longitude lines are 'long' — they run the long way, pole to pole. Together, a latitude and a longitude give a unique address for any point on Earth: Delhi is roughly 28.6° N, 77.2° E.

examples.t: A place at 0° latitude, 0° longitude
examples.d: The single point where the Equator meets the Prime Meridian, in the Gulf of Guinea off West Africa.

examples.t: Working out IST
examples.d: 82°30′ E × 4 minutes per degree = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

examples.t: Why Arunachal Pradesh sees sunrise before Gujarat
examples.d: Arunachal is further east. The Earth rotates west to east, so eastern longitudes meet the Sun first — about two hours earlier across India's width.

examples.t: The Tropic of Cancer in India
examples.d: 23½° N cuts across the middle of the country, passing through eight states including Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal and Mizoram.

mistakes: Calling the Prime Meridian a full circle. It is a semicircle from pole to pole; the Equator is the full circle.
Saying all parallels are equal in length. Only meridians are equal; parallels shrink towards the poles.
Writing that the Equator divides the Earth into east and west. It divides north and south — the Prime Meridian does east and west.
Forgetting that 1° of longitude equals 4 minutes of time, which is needed for every IST calculation.
Giving India's Standard Meridian as 82° E. It is 82°30′ E — the half degree is what makes IST 5:30 rather than 5:28.

quiz.q: The Equator divides the Earth into:
quiz.why: The Equator runs east-west at 0° latitude, separating the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. East and west are divided by the Prime Meridian.

quiz.q: India's Standard Meridian is:
quiz.why: 82°30′ E passes through Mirzapur; multiplying 82.5 by 4 minutes gives IST as GMT + 5:30.

quiz.q: How many parallels of latitude are there in total?
quiz.why: 90 in the Northern Hemisphere, 90 in the Southern, plus the Equator itself makes 181.

quiz.q: The Earth rotates through 1° of longitude in:
quiz.why: 360° in 24 hours is 15° per hour, so 1° takes 60 ÷ 15 = 4 minutes.

extraFaqs.q: Why was Greenwich chosen for the Prime Meridian?
extraFaqs.a: It was an international agreement, not a natural fact. At an 1884 conference the world agreed to place 0° longitude at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, largely because British nautical charts were already the most widely used. Any meridian could have been chosen instead.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between latitude and longitude?
extraFaqs.a: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, and its lines run east-west as parallels of unequal length. Longitude measures distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, and its lines run north-south as semicircles of equal length that meet at the poles.

extraFaqs.q: What is the International Date Line?
extraFaqs.a: It is roughly the 180° meridian, on the opposite side of the globe from the Prime Meridian. Crossing it changes the calendar date by one day. It bends in places so that island groups and countries are not split across two different dates.

extraFaqs.q: Why is Indian Standard Time 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT?
extraFaqs.a: India's Standard Meridian is 82°30′ E. Since the Earth turns 1° every 4 minutes, 82.5° × 4 = 330 minutes, which is 5 hours 30 minutes. A single standard meridian is used so the whole country keeps one time.

applications.h: Why India has one clock instead of two
applications.d: India stretches from about 68° E to 97° E — roughly 29 degrees of longitude, which at four minutes per degree means the sun rises in Arunachal Pradesh nearly two hours before it does in Gujarat. Running local time everywhere would be chaos for railways, broadcasting and flights, so India adopted a single Standard Meridian at 82°30′ E passing through Mirzapur, and every clock in the country is set to it. The cost is real: in the far north-east the sun can rise before 5 a.m. by the clock, which is why a separate north-eastern time zone is periodically debated.

applications.h: How latitude decides climate
applications.d: Latitude controls how directly sunlight strikes the ground, which is why the named parallels matter. Between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn the sun is overhead at some point in the year, giving the Torrid Zone its heat. Beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles the Frigid Zones receive only slanting rays. India is cut almost in half by the Tropic of Cancer at 23½° N, which is exactly why the south is tropical while the north has a distinct cold season.

applications.h: Finding any place on Earth
applications.d: A latitude and a longitude together give a unique address for any point on the planet — Delhi sits at roughly 28.6° N, 77.2° E. This is the basis of every GPS device, marine chart and aviation route. A ship reporting its position gives latitude first and longitude second, always with the hemisphere, because 28° N and 28° S are thousands of kilometres apart.

applications.h: The International Date Line and why it bends
applications.d: Roughly along the 180° meridian, on the opposite side of the globe from Greenwich, the calendar date changes by one day. Crossing it westward you lose a day; crossing eastward you gain one. It does not run perfectly straight: it bends around Siberia, the Aleutians and several Pacific island groups so that a single country is not split across two different dates — a neat illustration that longitude is a human convention laid over a physical rotation.

numericals.q: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich (0°), what is the local time at 82°30′ E?
steps: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 15° per hour, or 1° in 4 minutes.
The place is EAST of Greenwich, so its local time is AHEAD.
numericals.answer: 5:30 p.m. This is precisely why Indian Standard Time is GMT + 5:30.

numericals.q: A place lies at 60° W. If it is 6:00 p.m. GMT, what is the local time there?
steps: 1° of longitude corresponds to 4 minutes of time.
The place is WEST of Greenwich, so its local time is BEHIND GMT.
numericals.answer: 2:00 p.m. Remember: east is ahead, west is behind.

numericals.q: Two towns lie on the same parallel, one at 20° E and the other at 35° E. What is the difference in their local times?
steps: Each degree is 4 minutes of time.
numericals.answer: 1 hour. The town at 35° E is one hour ahead, because it lies further east and meets the sun first.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between the Equator and the Prime Meridian.
boardQuestions.a: The Equator is the imaginary line of 0° latitude drawn midway between the North and South Poles, dividing the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is a complete circle and the longest of all parallels, about 40,075 km around, and its position is fixed by the Earth itself. The Prime Meridian is the line of 0° longitude running from the North Pole to the South Pole through Greenwich near London, dividing the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. It is a semicircle, equal in length to every other meridian, and its position is a human choice agreed internationally in 1884 rather than a natural fact.

boardQuestions.q: Explain the relationship between longitude and time, using India as an example.
boardQuestions.a: The Earth completes one rotation of 360° in 24 hours, so it turns through 15° in one hour and through 1° in four minutes. Places to the east therefore see the sun earlier and their local time runs ahead, while places to the west lag behind. India extends from about 68° E to 97° E, so local time at the eastern edge is nearly two hours ahead of the western edge. To avoid the confusion of many local times, India adopted 82°30′ E, passing through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, as its Standard Meridian. Since 82.5 × 4 minutes = 330 minutes, Indian Standard Time is fixed at 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time, and all clocks in the country follow it.

boardQuestions.q: What are the heat zones of the Earth? Name them and give the latitudes that bound each.
boardQuestions.a: There are three heat zones, defined by how directly the sun’s rays strike the surface. The Torrid Zone lies between the Tropic of Cancer at 23½° N and the Tropic of Capricorn at 23½° S; the midday sun is directly overhead here at least once a year, so it receives the greatest heat. The two Temperate Zones lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle at 66½° N in the north, and between the Tropic of Capricorn and the Antarctic Circle at 66½° S in the south; the sun is never directly overhead and temperatures are moderate. The two Frigid Zones lie beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles, extending to the poles; the sun’s rays are always very slanting and these are the coldest regions.

boardQuestions.q: State three differences between parallels of latitude and meridians of longitude.
boardQuestions.a: First, parallels of latitude run in an east-west direction and are complete circles, while meridians of longitude run north-south from pole to pole and are semicircles. Second, parallels are unequal in length — the Equator is the longest and they shrink to a point at each pole — whereas all meridians are equal in length. Third, parallels never meet one another and are always the same distance apart, while all meridians converge and meet at the two poles. A fourth accepted difference is that there are 181 parallels in total but 360 meridians.

boardQuestions.q: Why was the Prime Meridian fixed at Greenwich?
boardQuestions.a: There is nothing physically special about Greenwich; unlike the Equator, whose position is determined by the Earth’s own axis of rotation, the zero of longitude had to be chosen. At an international conference in 1884 the world agreed to place 0° longitude at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, largely because British nautical charts were already the most widely used and many countries had adopted them in practice. Any other meridian could have been chosen instead.

assertionReason.assertion: All meridians of longitude are equal in length.
assertionReason.reason: Meridians run from the North Pole to the South Pole and meet at the poles.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. Because every meridian spans the same pole-to-pole distance, they are all the same length — unlike parallels, which shrink towards the poles.

assertionReason.assertion: Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
assertionReason.reason: India’s Standard Meridian is 82°30′ E and the Earth rotates 1° in 4 minutes.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason is the exact calculation behind the assertion: 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes.

assertionReason.assertion: The Equator divides the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
assertionReason.reason: The Equator is the longest parallel of latitude.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false — the Equator divides the Northern from the Southern Hemisphere; east and west are divided by the Prime Meridian. The reason is true but unrelated to the false assertion.

assertionReason.assertion: Places east of a given meridian have a later local time than places west of it.
assertionReason.reason: The Earth rotates from west to east.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. Because the Earth turns west to east, eastern longitudes meet the sun first, so their local time is ahead.

glossary.def: The imaginary circle of 0° latitude midway between the poles, dividing the Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
The semicircle of 0° longitude through Greenwich, dividing the Earth into Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
Angular distance north or south of the Equator, measured in degrees. Its lines run east-west.
Angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured in degrees. Its lines run north-south.
A line of latitude. There are 181 in total — 90 north, 90 south, plus the Equator.
A line of longitude. There are 360 in total — 180 east and 180 west of the Prime Meridian.
23½° N. It passes through eight Indian states, cutting the country roughly in half.
23½° S, the southern limit of the Torrid Zone.
66½° N, the boundary of the northern Frigid Zone.
The meridian whose local time a whole country adopts. India’s is 82°30′ E, through Mirzapur.
Roughly the 180° meridian, where the calendar date changes by one day. It bends to avoid splitting countries.
The hottest heat zone, between the two Tropics, where the sun is overhead at some point each year.

revision: EQUATOR = 0° LATITUDE, splits NORTH/SOUTH, a full circle, the longest parallel (~40,075 km).
PRIME MERIDIAN = 0° LONGITUDE, splits EAST/WEST, a semicircle through Greenwich, chosen in 1884.
181 parallels (90 N + 90 S + Equator). 360 meridians (180 E + 180 W).
Parallels are UNEQUAL and never meet. Meridians are EQUAL and all meet at the poles.
1° of longitude = 4 minutes of time. 15° = 1 hour. East is AHEAD, west is BEHIND.
Named parallels: Tropic of Cancer 23½° N, Capricorn 23½° S, Arctic 66½° N, Antarctic 66½° S.
Heat zones: Torrid (between Tropics), two Temperate, two Frigid (beyond the Circles).

square-and-cube.ncertRef: NCERT Class 8 Maths, Chapter 6 — Squares and Square Roots and Chapter 7 — Cubes and Cube Roots; shapes covered in Class 8 Chapter 10 — Visualising Solid Shapes.

explainers.term: This question has two different answers — check which one you need
paras: 'Difference between square and cube' is asked in two quite separate senses, and answering the wrong one loses full marks. The first sense is arithmetic: squaring a number versus cubing it. The second is geometric: the square as a flat 2D shape versus the cube as a 3D solid.

Both are on the CBSE syllabus and both are covered below. If the question mentions numbers, roots or exponents, it is the arithmetic sense. If it mentions faces, edges, vertices, area or volume, it is the shape sense.

explainers.term: Sense 1 — squaring versus cubing a number
paras: The square of a number is that number multiplied by itself once: n² = n × n. So 5² = 25. The cube is the number multiplied by itself twice more: n³ = n × n × n. So 5³ = 125.

The exponent is the only difference in the formula, but the growth rates diverge fast. For n = 10, the square is 100 and the cube is 1,000. For n = 20, the square is 400 and the cube is 8,000 — twenty times larger. This is why volume grows so much faster than area when an object is scaled up.

explainers.term: Sense 2 — the square shape versus the cube solid
paras: A square is a two-dimensional (flat) shape with four equal sides and four right angles. It has length and breadth but no thickness, so it has area but no volume.

A cube is a three-dimensional solid built from six identical square faces. It has length, breadth and height, so it has both surface area and volume. A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. In effect, a square is one face of a cube — the cube is what you get when a square is given depth.

sections.h: The formulas you need for both
paras: Learn these as pairs; questions very often ask for one of each.
bullets: Square of a number: n² = n × n. Square root: √n, the number which when squared gives n.
Cube of a number: n³ = n × n × n. Cube root: ∛n, the number which when cubed gives n.
Square shape, side a: Area = a², Perimeter = 4a, Diagonal = a√2.
Cube solid, edge a: Volume = a³, Total surface area = 6a², Lateral surface area = 4a², Space diagonal = a√3.

sections.h: Properties of square numbers that save time in exams
paras: These let you reject wrong options instantly in an MCQ, without calculating.
bullets: A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. If a number ends in one of those digits, it cannot be a perfect square.
A perfect square never has an odd number of zeros at the end. 100 is a perfect square; 1000 is not.
The square of an even number is even; the square of an odd number is odd.
Squares are never negative. Cubes can be — (−4)³ = −64, while (−4)² = +16. This sign behaviour is the most examined difference between the two operations.
The sum of the first n odd numbers equals n². For example 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4².

sections.h: Perfect squares and perfect cubes to memorise
paras: Notice that 1 and 64 appear in both lists — they are both perfect squares and perfect cubes (64 = 8² = 4³). The next such number is 729 = 27² = 9³.

examples.t: Square and cube of 7
examples.d: 7² = 49. 7³ = 343. The cube is seven times the square, which is always true: n³ = n² × n.

examples.t: A square tile of side 5 cm
examples.d: Area = 5² = 25 cm². Perimeter = 4 × 5 = 20 cm. There is no volume — the tile is treated as flat.

examples.t: A cubical box of edge 5 cm
examples.d: Volume = 5³ = 125 cm³. Total surface area = 6 × 5² = 150 cm². It has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

examples.t: Why sign matters
examples.d: (−3)² = 9, but (−3)³ = −27. Squaring destroys the negative sign; cubing keeps it.

mistakes: Answering only the number sense when the question meant the shapes, or vice versa. Read the question for the words 'faces', 'volume' or 'area'.
Writing the total surface area of a cube as 4a². That is the lateral surface area; the total is 6a² because a cube has six faces.
Assuming a cube is 'a square in 3D' and therefore has 4 faces. It has 6.
Thinking a cube of a negative number is positive. Only even powers force a positive result.
Mixing up a cube (all edges equal) with a cuboid (a box whose length, breadth and height can differ).

quiz.q: What is the cube of 6?
quiz.why: 6³ = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216. 36 is the square, and 1296 is 6⁴.

quiz.q: How many edges does a cube have?
quiz.why: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

quiz.q: Which of these cannot be a perfect square?
quiz.why: 128 ends in 8, and no perfect square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8.

quiz.q: The total surface area of a cube of edge 4 cm is:
quiz.why: Total surface area = 6a² = 6 × 16 = 96 cm². 64 cm³ would be its volume.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a square and a cube?
extraFaqs.a: In arithmetic, the square of a number multiplies it by itself once (n² = n × n) while the cube multiplies it by itself twice more (n³ = n × n × n). In geometry, a square is a flat 2D shape with four equal sides and only area, while a cube is a 3D solid made of six square faces with both surface area and volume.

extraFaqs.q: Is a cube made of squares?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. A cube is bounded by six identical square faces. That is why its total surface area is 6a² — six squares, each of area a².

extraFaqs.q: Can a number be both a perfect square and a perfect cube?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. Such numbers are perfect sixth powers. The first few are 1, 64 (which is 8² and 4³) and 729 (which is 27² and 9³).

extraFaqs.q: Why is the cube of a negative number negative?
extraFaqs.a: Cubing multiplies three negative factors together. Two negatives give a positive, and the third negative makes the result negative again. Squaring uses only two factors, so the negatives always cancel and the answer is positive.

applications.h: Why volume grows faster than area
applications.d: Double the side of a cube and its surface area goes up four times but its volume goes up eight times, because area depends on a² and volume on a³. This single fact explains a great deal: why a large ice block melts more slowly than the same mass crushed into cubes (less surface per unit volume), why small animals lose body heat faster than large ones, and why a giant version of an insect could not actually support its own weight. Engineers call this the square-cube law.

applications.h: Squares and cubes in everyday measurement
applications.d: Whenever you buy floor tiles you are working in squares — area is measured in square metres, and the number of tiles needed depends on a². Whenever you buy water, sand or a storage tank you are working in cubes — volume is measured in cubic metres, and a tank twice as tall, wide and deep holds eight times as much. Confusing the two units, m² and m³, is the most expensive arithmetic mistake in ordinary life.

applications.h: Pythagoras and squares
applications.d: The theorem you use constantly in geometry is literally a statement about squares: in a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, a² + b² = c². The famous 3-4-5 triangle works because 9 + 16 = 25. Recognising perfect squares instantly — 25, 144, 169 — is what lets you spot these triples in an exam without a calculator.

applications.h: Cube roots in packing and design
applications.d: If a cubical carton must hold 1,000 cm³, its edge is the cube root of 1,000, which is 10 cm. Working backwards from a required volume to a dimension is exactly what cube roots are for, and it is the reason the cube-root table up to 10 is worth memorising. The same reasoning sizes water tanks, shipping crates and storage boxes.

numericals.q: Find the smallest number by which 392 must be multiplied to make it a perfect cube.
steps: For a perfect cube every prime must appear in groups of three.
2 appears three times — complete. 7 appears only twice, so it needs one more.
numericals.answer: 7. The resulting cube is 2744, whose cube root is 14.

numericals.q: Find the square root of 1024 by prime factorisation.
steps: For a square root, take the primes in PAIRS.

numericals.q: The volume of a cube is 216 cm³. Find its edge, total surface area and the length of one face diagonal.
steps: A face is a square of side 6 cm, so its diagonal = a√2 = 6√2 cm ≈ 8.49 cm.
numericals.answer: Edge 6 cm, total surface area 216 cm², face diagonal 6√2 ≈ 8.49 cm. Note the volume and surface area are numerically equal here (216) but the UNITS differ — cm³ against cm².

numericals.q: Without calculating, decide which of 1057, 23453, 7928 and 222222 can be perfect squares.
steps: A perfect square never ends in the digits 2, 3, 7 or 8.
1057 ends in 7 — cannot be a perfect square.
23453 ends in 3 — cannot be a perfect square.
7928 ends in 8 — cannot be a perfect square.
222222 ends in 2 — cannot be a perfect square.
numericals.answer: None of them. All four end in 2, 3, 7 or 8, so all are ruled out instantly without any calculation.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between the square and the cube of a number, and between a square and a cube as shapes.
boardQuestions.a: As an operation on numbers, the square of a number multiplies it by itself once, written n² = n × n, so 5² = 25. The cube multiplies it by itself twice more, written n³ = n × n × n, so 5³ = 125. As shapes, a square is a two-dimensional figure with four equal sides and four right angles; it has length and breadth only, so it has area (a²) and perimeter (4a) but no volume. A cube is a three-dimensional solid bounded by six identical square faces, with length, breadth and height, so it has volume (a³) and total surface area (6a²), along with 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

boardQuestions.q: State four properties of perfect squares.
boardQuestions.a: First, a perfect square never ends in the digits 2, 3, 7 or 8, which lets you rule out numbers instantly. Second, a perfect square never has an odd number of zeros at the end — 100 is a perfect square but 1000 is not. Third, the square of an even number is always even and the square of an odd number is always odd. Fourth, the sum of the first n odd natural numbers is always n²; for example 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4². A fifth acceptable property is that squares are never negative, since multiplying two numbers of the same sign always gives a positive result.

boardQuestions.q: A cubical tank of edge 2 m is filled with water. Find its capacity in litres and its total surface area.
boardQuestions.a: The volume of a cube is a³, so the capacity is 2³ = 8 cubic metres. Since 1 cubic metre equals 1000 litres, the tank holds 8 × 1000 = 8000 litres. The total surface area of a cube is 6a², so it is 6 × 2² = 6 × 4 = 24 square metres. Note carefully that volume is measured in m³ and surface area in m², and that the lateral surface area would be 4a² = 16 m² if only the four walls were required.

boardQuestions.q: Explain why the cube of a negative number is negative but its square is positive.
boardQuestions.a: Squaring multiplies two identical factors together. When both are negative, their product is positive, because a negative times a negative gives a positive; so (−3)² = 9. Cubing multiplies three identical factors. The first two negatives give a positive, and multiplying that positive by the third negative factor makes the result negative; so (−3)³ = −27. In general, an even power of a negative number is positive and an odd power is negative.

boardQuestions.q: Find the smallest number by which 3087 must be divided to obtain a perfect cube.
boardQuestions.a: First find the prime factorisation. 3087 = 3 × 1029 = 3 × 3 × 343 = 3² × 7³. For a perfect cube, each prime must occur in groups of three. Here 7 occurs three times, which is complete, but 3 occurs only twice, which is an incomplete group. Dividing by 3² = 9 removes the incomplete group entirely, giving 3087 ÷ 9 = 343 = 7³, which is a perfect cube with cube root 7. The required smallest number is therefore 9.

assertionReason.assertion: A number ending in 8 cannot be a perfect square.
assertionReason.reason: Perfect squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Squaring any digit 0-9 produces a last digit only from that set, so 2, 3, 7 and 8 are impossible endings.

assertionReason.assertion: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
assertionReason.reason: A cube is a prism with a square base.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true — a cube is indeed a square prism — but the reason is not the explanation of the specific counts, which follow from the prism formulas n+2 faces, 3n edges and 2n vertices with n = 4.

assertionReason.assertion: The volume and the total surface area of a cube of edge 6 can be compared directly.
assertionReason.reason: Both work out to the number 216.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false: the two quantities have different dimensions, cm³ against cm², so they cannot be compared even when the numbers coincide. The reason is a true arithmetic statement, which is exactly what makes this a good trap.

assertionReason.assertion: 64 is both a perfect square and a perfect cube.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason demonstrates the assertion. Such numbers are perfect sixth powers; the next one is 729 = 27² = 9³.

glossary.def: The number multiplied by itself once: n² = n × n. So 7² = 49.
The number multiplied by itself twice more: n³ = n × n × n. So 7³ = 343.
The number which, when squared, gives the original. Written √n. √49 = 7.
The number which, when cubed, gives the original. Written ∛n. ∛343 = 7.
A number that is the square of a whole number, such as 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
A number that is the cube of a whole number, such as 1, 8, 27, 64, 125.
A 2D figure with four equal sides and four right angles. Area a², perimeter 4a, diagonal a√2.
A 3D solid with six identical square faces. Volume a³, total surface area 6a², 12 edges, 8 vertices.
A box-shaped solid whose length, breadth and height may all differ. A cube is the special case where all three are equal.
The area of the side faces only, excluding the top and bottom. For a cube it is 4a².
Writing a number as a product of primes. Grouping those primes in pairs gives square roots, in threes gives cube roots.
When a solid is scaled up, its area grows as the square of the scale factor but its volume as the cube.

revision: TWO meanings — check whether the question is about NUMBERS or SHAPES before answering.
Numbers: n² = n × n (one extra factor). n³ = n × n × n (two extra factors). n³ = n² × n.
Shapes: SQUARE is 2D with area only. CUBE is 3D with volume AND surface area.
Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. Volume a³, TOTAL surface 6a², LATERAL 4a².
Square: area a², perimeter 4a, diagonal a√2. Cube space diagonal a√3.
A perfect square NEVER ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8 — use this to eliminate MCQ options instantly.
Squares are never negative. Cubes keep the sign: (−4)² = +16 but (−4)³ = −64.
1 and 64 are both perfect squares AND perfect cubes. So is 729 = 27² = 9³.

transpiration-and-translocation.ncertRef: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 6 — Life Processes (transport in plants); introduced in Class 7, Chapter 11.

explainers.term: Transpiration — losing water on purpose
paras: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly the leaves. Most of it escapes through tiny pores called stomata, each guarded by a pair of bean-shaped guard cells that open the pore when they swell with water and close it when they lose water.

It sounds wasteful — a large tree can lose hundreds of litres a day — but the plant gains three things from it. It creates the suction that pulls water up from the roots, it cools the leaf in the way sweating cools you, and it carries dissolved minerals upward with the water stream.

explainers.term: Translocation — moving food where it is needed
paras: Translocation is the transport of the soluble products of photosynthesis — mainly sucrose, along with amino acids — from where they are made to where they are needed. It happens in the phloem, and unlike transpiration it costs the plant energy in the form of ATP.

The tissue that supplies the food is called the source, usually a green leaf. The part that receives it is the sink — a root, a growing shoot tip, a developing fruit or a storage organ. Because sinks exist above and below the leaves, translocation moves food both upward and downward, which is the detail students most often get wrong.

sections.h: Xylem versus phloem — the two transport tissues
paras: Almost every question on this topic reduces to knowing which tissue does what. Learn these as a contrasting pair.
bullets: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals. Phloem carries prepared food (sucrose).
Xylem moves material only upward, from root to leaf. Phloem moves food in both directions, source to sink.
Xylem is made of dead cells — tracheids and vessels with no living contents, which is why it forms hollow tubes. Phloem is made of living cells — sieve tubes and their companion cells.
Xylem transport is passive: no energy is spent, because transpiration pull does the work. Phloem transport is active and needs ATP.
Xylem elements are lignified for strength; phloem sieve tubes have perforated sieve plates that let material pass between cells.

sections.h: How transpiration pull actually lifts water
paras: As water evaporates from the leaf surface, it leaves the cells there slightly short of water. That creates a suction, and because water molecules stick to one another (cohesion) and to the xylem walls (adhesion), the whole column of water in the xylem is pulled upward as one continuous thread.

This suction force is called transpiration pull, and it is strong enough to raise water to the top of the tallest trees without the plant spending any energy. It is the reason transpiration is described as a necessary evil rather than simply a loss.

sections.h: What changes the rate of transpiration
paras: The factors mirror those for evaporation, because transpiration is evaporation happening through a leaf.
bullets: Temperature — higher temperature speeds it up.
Humidity — high humidity slows it down, since the surrounding air already holds water vapour.
Wind speed — moving air carries vapour away and speeds it up.
Light — stomata open in light and close in the dark, so transpiration is much higher during the day.
Available soil water — a plant short of water closes its stomata to conserve what it has.

examples.t: Water droplets inside a polythene bag tied over a leafy shoot
examples.d: Transpiration. Water vapour left the leaves and condensed on the cool plastic.

examples.t: Sugar reaching a developing mango
examples.d: Translocation. The fruit is a sink; sucrose made in the leaves travels to it through the phloem.

examples.t: A wilting plant at noon
examples.d: Transpiration is outpacing absorption, so the cells lose turgor. The plant closes its stomata to slow the loss.

examples.t: A potato tuber swelling underground
examples.d: Translocation moving food downward to a storage sink — proof that phloem transport is not one-directional.

mistakes: Saying translocation happens in the xylem. Food moves in the phloem; the xylem carries water and minerals.
Writing that translocation only moves food downwards. It moves to any sink, above or below the leaves.
Calling transpiration simply a waste of water. It generates the transpiration pull that lifts water and it cools the plant.
Forgetting that phloem transport needs energy while xylem transport does not.
Confusing guttation with transpiration — guttation is the loss of liquid water droplets from leaf margins, not water vapour.

quiz.q: Food prepared in the leaves is transported through the:
quiz.why: Phloem carries the soluble products of photosynthesis from source to sink. Xylem carries water and minerals.

quiz.q: Transpiration mainly takes place through:
quiz.why: Stomata are the pores on leaves through which most water vapour escapes.

quiz.q: Which statement about xylem is correct?
options: It is made of living cells
It is made of dead cells and moves water upward
quiz.why: Xylem consists of dead, lignified tracheids and vessels, and moves water upward passively using transpiration pull.

quiz.q: Translocation requires energy because:
options: It is an active process using ATP
quiz.why: Phloem loading and unloading are active processes that consume ATP, unlike passive xylem transport.

extraFaqs.q: Is transpiration a necessary evil?
extraFaqs.a: Yes, and that is the phrase textbooks use. The plant loses a great deal of water, which is the 'evil' part. But the loss generates the transpiration pull that raises water from the roots, cools the leaves, and carries dissolved minerals upward — so the plant cannot do without it.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between the source and the sink in translocation?
extraFaqs.a: The source is the part that makes or releases food, usually a photosynthesising leaf. The sink is any part that uses or stores it — roots, growing tips, flowers, fruits and storage organs. Food always moves from source to sink, which can be in any direction.

extraFaqs.q: Why does transpiration decrease in humid weather?
extraFaqs.a: The surrounding air already holds a lot of water vapour, so the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the air is small. With a weaker gradient, less water evaporates from the leaf surface.

extraFaqs.q: What is guttation and how is it different from transpiration?
extraFaqs.a: Guttation is the loss of liquid water as droplets from the margins of leaves, usually at night or early morning when humidity is high and root pressure is strong. Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour, mainly through stomata during the day.
